clue.text: Bad language used in charging second barrier

parts.note: charging a customer is billing them
a gate is a barrier across an opening

explanation.surface: Swearing breaks out as someone is billed for a second fence.
explanation.walkthrough: BILLINGSGATE was London's fish market, whose porters were famous for their foul mouths, hence the word for coarse abuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse, abusive talk is named after the London fish market whose traders swore freely.

clue.text: More than one engagement for Ben and Sarah?

explanation.surface: A couple named Ben and Sarah seem to have had several engagements.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Battle is the soldier of Thomas Hood's comic ballad 'Faithless Nelly Gray'; Sarah Battle is the whist-playing lady of Charles Lamb's essay. Together they are two people sharing one surname, in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Engagements are fights in military language; the second sense is the plural of a family surname shared by two literary characters.

clue.text: Some popular gentlemen are so generous

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Well-liked men are said to be lavish with their money.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'are so generous' as the definition, but that is a verb phrase and cannot stand in for an adjective; 'are so' is the link and 'generous' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Large in the old sense of open-handed, as in 'large-hearted', means liberal with gifts.

clue.text: Not fair to have elected Attlee?

parts.note: a candidate who is elected is in office
Clement Attlee was the British Labour Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that voting Attlee in was an unfair result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fair' reads as a complaint about justice, but it is weather: an inclement day is not fair. Clement Attlee was a British Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather that is harsh, stormy or cold is described as the opposite of fair.

clue.text: English poet's gloomy spell in America

explanation.surface: An English poet goes through a dark patch while in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote the 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'. The second definition is a pun: GRAY is how Americans spell the colour, and 'spell' means spelling, not a period of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray was an eighteenth-century English poet; the American spelling of the dull colour of overcast skies drops the British E.

clue.text: Note a little unnatural radiation

parts.note: G is one of the musical notes A to G
slight means small or little

explanation.surface: A musical note carries a faint trace of artificial radiation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamps burning coal gas gave artificial light, light not from a natural source.

clue.text: Tribute in honour of a saint

parts.note: one drinks to someone in their honour

explanation.surface: A tribute is paid in honour of some holy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising glasses and drinking to someone is a spoken tribute paid at a celebration.

clue.text: With a single exception, it's included for singer

indicators.note: included says the word it is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'
a single means one
the word it, with its 's read as is

explanation.surface: Apart from one, it is included in the choir for a vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With a single exception' is the idiom 'all bar one'; 'included' slips the pronoun in after the first word of that phrase. 'Singer' is a voice type here.
explanation.definitionFit: A man whose voice lies between bass and tenor is a kind of vocalist.

clue.text: Hot shawl, latest in fashion

parts.note: a stole is a long scarf or shawl worn over the shoulders

indicators.note: latest in picks the final letter of the word fashion

explanation.surface: A shawl is the hottest new thing in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' looks like fashionable, matching the surface; it means stolen goods, as in 'hot property'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is slang for goods recently taken by theft and risky to handle.

clue.text: Contrast oddly with upper-class deserters

indicators.note: oddly signals that the letters are arranged in a strange new order

explanation.surface: Posh deserters make a strange contrast with the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' shuffles CONTRAST together with U into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who switches sides abandons their party or cause, like a traitor.

clue.text: One way to make a mammoth stop!

parts.note: mammoth means huge, vast

explanation.surface: A cry for someone to halt a woolly mammoth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One way to make' is the link: one way to put together 'a mammoth' is A + VAST. AVAST is a sailor's call to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Avast is the old nautical command to cease or hold what one is doing.

clue.text: German works as guide for audience

indicators.note: for an audience means the word is heard rather than read, so it sounds like another

parts.note: a leader is one who guides

explanation.surface: A German piece serves as a guide for listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: LIEDER are German art songs, as by Schubert; they sound like LEADER.
explanation.definitionFit: These are German art songs, musical compositions for voice and piano.

clue.text: It isn't just one in the wind

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the mistral is the cold north wind of southern France
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Something unfair seems to be blowing in the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The MISTRAL is a named wind of southern France; I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial voided by an error in procedure is one that fails to deliver justice.

clue.text: Shoot — easy target

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fire at a target that cannot be missed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant's side growth from the root is called a shoot; a gullible person is a mug, easily fooled.

clue.text: Is one able to admit one saint thus?

parts.note: can means is able

indicators.note: to admit means to let something in, so these letters are placed inside

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether one may admit somebody to sainthood this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint' is a verb here, meaning to make someone a saint; 'one' (second time) and 'thus' are link words. 'to admit' signals the container, read with 'able' first.
explanation.definitionFit: To saint someone, as a verb, is to declare them holy by official church decree.

clue.text: Brought back to earth, being defeated in argument?

explanation.surface: Someone is deflated after losing a debate.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane hit by fire falls from the sky; a proposal or speaker rejected in debate has also been knocked out.

clue.text: Protective covering intended, we hear, for book collection

parts.note: a testa is the hard outer coat that protects a seed

indicators.note: we hear says a word is heard, so it sounds like another spelling

parts.note: meant means intended

explanation.surface: A dust jacket is designed for a set of books.
explanation.walkthrough: A TESTA is a seed's protective coat. Old and New Testaments are the collections of books making up the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Each half of the Bible gathers many separate books into a single scripture.

clue.text: Part of Twelfth Night badly translated? Nothing's right after first volume

indicators.note: right after says the next letter comes immediately after the piece before

parts.note: mal is French for badly
volume one is written VOL I
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A poor translation of Shakespeare's comedy gets things right only after its first volume.
explanation.walkthrough: MALVOLIO is the pompous steward in Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night'; 'part' means a role, not a section of the play.
explanation.definitionFit: This role is the puritanical steward tricked into wearing yellow stockings in Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: Boy with appeal, so to speak

explanation.surface: An attractive young lad.
explanation.walkthrough: A Jonathan is a variety of apple, and an apple comes 'with a peel', which said quickly is 'with appeal'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a boy's given name; it is also an apple variety, fruit that has a skin, a pun on its sound.

clue.text: Raise a pound for one doing the dirty work

parts.note: to jack something up is to raise it
L stands for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone raises a pound by doing an unpleasant job.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackal is a lackey who does menial or shady tasks for a master, like the animal said to find prey for lions.

clue.text: Totally inactive as huntsman after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word is read in reverse order

parts.note: John Peel was the famous Cumbrian huntsman of the song 'D'ye ken John Peel'

explanation.surface: A huntsman who has retired does nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel is the huntsman of the English folk song 'D'ye ken John Peel'; 'after retiring' turns his name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sleeping is wholly at rest, doing nothing at all.

clue.text: Stone Age, nonetheless, precedes the first 16

indicators.note: precedes says this piece goes before the next
read as none less: nought, the letter O, taken away

parts.note: an age is a period of time
16 is the answer TESTAMENT, and the first of the two is the Old Testament, abbreviated OT

explanation.surface: Even so, the Stone Age comes before something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nonetheless' splits as 'none less': the period loses its nought. 16 is the Bible answer, and its first part is the Old one. 'Stone Age' looks like one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Peridot is a green gemstone, a variety of the mineral olivine.

clue.text: Provide protection? Do, do!

parts.note: to do someone is to swindle or con them
do means serve, as in 'that will do'

explanation.surface: An urgent plea to protect something: just do it!
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'do's are different senses: to swindle, and to suffice.
explanation.definitionFit: To conserve something is to keep it safe and preserve it from harm.

clue.text: Elizabeth's favourite county

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth's best-loved shire.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, was the favourite of Elizabeth I; Essex is also a county east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl who was a court darling of Elizabeth I shares his title with an English shire beside London.

clue.text: Short sword or dagger? It depends!

explanation.surface: Asked whether to bring a sword or a dagger, someone replies that it depends.
explanation.walkthrough: A hanger was a short sword hung from the belt; the second definition plays on 'depend', which literally means to hang down.
explanation.definitionFit: It was a short sword hung from a belt; and a thing that hangs from something can be said to depend from it.

clue.text: A stage for Shakespeare?

parts.note: both the London playhouse where his plays were performed and the world, which he called a stage in 'As You Like It'

explanation.surface: Somewhere Shakespeare's plays might be acted.
explanation.walkthrough: The Globe was Shakespeare's theatre on London's South Bank; Jaques in 'As You Like It' says 'All the world's a stage'.
explanation.definitionFit: The playhouse was where his company acted, and the world itself was his stage in a famous speech.

clue.text: Polish composer's friend — a Pole, also

parts.note: S stands for the South Pole
and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: A friend of a composer from Poland is himself a Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: George Sand was the French novelist who was Chopin's companion; Chopin is the Polish composer. 'Polish' wants to be the verb to polish, which SAND could also mean.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist George Sand was the lover and companion of Chopin, the composer from Poland.

clue.text: Fools given old coins

explanation.surface: Idiots are handed antique money.
explanation.definitionFit: Donkeys stand for stupid people; the as was a Roman bronze coin, so several are called by this plural.

clue.text: Liberal moderate with influence in the land, sort of

parts.note: to ease something is to moderate or lessen it
a hold over someone is influence over them

explanation.surface: A moderate Liberal with clout in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a leasehold is a kind of tenure, a stake held in land for a fixed term.
explanation.definitionFit: A leasehold is a property interest held for a term of years under a lease, a form of tenure.

clue.text: Way in which colleges may be found in London area?

definitions.text: Way in which colleges may be found in London area?

parts.words: Way in which colleges may be found in London area
parts.note: a road in central London named after the university city full of colleges, read as if the colleges lay along it

explanation.surface: Asking where in London a university's colleges are located.
explanation.walkthrough: OXFORD STREET is London's main shopping street; the city of Oxford is famous for its university colleges.
explanation.definitionFit: The London shopping road bears the name of the English university city made up of colleges.
